problems.title: The bounded-loss transfer coefficient is too small
claim: For \(0\le f\le C\), the paper bounds transferred loss by distilled loss plus \(C\sqrt{\mathrm{KL}(P\|Q)}/(2\sqrt2)\).
analysis: Let the input be a singleton, \(Q(Y)=P_{\rm tr}(Y)=(4/5,1/5)\), balanced \(P_{\rm te}(Y)=(1/2,1/2)\), and classifier \(\widehat p=(4/5,1/5)\). Label shift holds and \(C=\log5\). Direct evaluation gives \(\ell_Q=0.50040242\), \(\ell_{\rm te}=0.91629073\) and \(\mathrm{KL}(P_{\rm te}\|Q)=\log(5/4)\). The printed right side is \(0.76919756\), strictly below the actual loss. The general bounded-loss argument is \(E_Pf-E_Qf\le C\operatorname{TV}(P,Q)\le C\sqrt{\mathrm{KL}(P\|Q)/2}\); its coefficient is twice the printed one.
result: The displayed transfer guarantee is false on a strictly positive admissible two-class model. The corrected coefficient retains a population transfer bound but does not reproduce the ADSA accuracy gains.
repair: Replace the coefficient by \(C/\sqrt2\) and use the bounded-loss/total-variation argument. This corrects the numerical guarantee without proving the calibration algorithm optimal.
problems.impact_rationale: A central quantitative theorem used to motivate the method is explicitly false under its own assumptions, although a weaker bound survives.
problems.existing_correction_status: The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Training and test joint KL are identified despite label shift
claim: The discrepancy defined from the training law is called equivalent to decompositions based on the balanced test law.
analysis: On the singleton-input example \(P_{\rm tr}=Q=(4/5,1/5)\) and \(P_{\rm te}=(1/2,1/2)\), the original joint KL is \(0\), while the proposed prior-plus-conditional decomposition is \(\log(5/4)>0\). With \(Q=(1/2,1/2)\), the original KL becomes \(0.19274476\) and the test-law KL becomes \(0\). The difference changes with \(Q\), so a constant independent of the distilled law cannot repair equality.
result: The theorem changes which distributional discrepancy is being optimized. Both ordinary KL chain rules remain valid when consistently applied to the test joint.
repair: Define \(R_{\rm te}=\mathrm{KL}(P_{\rm te}(X,Y)\|Q(X,Y))\) explicitly; its feature/posterior and prior/conditional chain-rule decompositions are exact. Use this new quantity in the corrected population bound.
problems.impact_rationale: The stated equivalence in the central theorem fails and substitutes a different optimization target, beyond a harmless normalization error.
problems.existing_correction_status: The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: A balanced prior does not imply matched conditional features
claim: The appendix infers zero conditional and feature-marginal KL from a uniform test class prior.
analysis: Use \(P_{\rm tr}(Y)=(4/5,1/5)\), \(P_{\rm te}(Y)=Q(Y)=(1/2,1/2)\), and for both classes \(P_{\rm tr}(X\mid y)=P_{\rm te}(X\mid y)=(4/5,1/5)\), \(Q(X\mid y)=(1/5,4/5)\). All masses are positive and label shift holds. Each conditional KL and the feature-marginal KL equal \((3/5)\log4>0\), while the class-prior KL is \(0\).
result: The zero-discrepancy simplification requires successful conditional distribution matching in addition to equal class counts. The example does not show equal IPC or calibration is practically ineffective.
repair: State equality of every class-conditional distribution as an additional premise. Positive uniform prior weights then make the conditional KL sum zero exactly when each conditional matches.
problems.impact_rationale: This invalid ideal-limit inference needs an additional distribution-matching premise; it does not independently refute the empirical procedure.
problems.existing_correction_status: The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

impact_rationale: Major: explicit admissible distributions falsify the central transfer inequality and its claimed discrepancy equivalence, while empirical accuracy remains untested.
